prompt.context: A major producer of juice is in the business of processing and packaging fruit juice for retail outlets. Traditionally, the producer has packaged the juice in 18-ounce carton containers. Recently, in response to demand from the market, the producer purchased a machine that packages the juice in plastic gallons (36 ounces). Over the next couple of years, sales continued to grow on average of 20% per year. Yet, as sales continued to increase, profits steadily decreased.
prompt.question: The owner cannot understand why profits are declining despite growing sales. He hires you to help out. Why are profits declining, and what should the owner do?

clarifying_info.q: How much does the producer charge for the 18 oz. carton?
How much does the producer charge for the 36 oz. plastic gallon?
clarifying_info.a: Initially $3.50 per gallon; later raised to $4.00 after adding a $0.50 price increase across the board.

clarifying_info.q: How was the cost of the new equipment accounted for in pricing?
clarifying_info.a: The producer raised prices across the board by $0.50 on all packages — both cartons and gallons — resulting in prices of $2.50 and $4.00 respectively.

clarifying_info.q: Does it cost the same to package juice in cartons versus plastic gallons?
clarifying_info.a: No. Plastic is more expensive than the paper carton traditionally used. Additionally, more experienced (and expensive) labor was required to operate the new machine. The producer assumed increased volume from gallons would cover the costs.
All factory costs are added together and divided by the number of units produced (i.e., a simple per-unit average across all products).

clarifying_info.q: What is the sales mix between cartons and gallons?
clarifying_info.a: As overall volume has grown, plastic gallons have comprised 60% of sales. The owner has been very pleased about this trend.

framework: Use the profitability framework: Revenue = Price x Volume; Profit = Revenue - Costs
Confirm revenue is growing (sales up 20% per year) — the issue must lie on the cost side
Investigate pricing: compare price per ounce across the two SKUs to check for under-pricing
Investigate cost structure: determine whether packaging costs and labor costs differ by SKU
Investigate cost allocation method: understand how overhead is spread across products
Identify the sales mix and assess whether the higher-cost product is appropriately priced

questions.prompt: Is the revenue side the source of the problem?
questions.guidance: Sales are growing at 20% per year, so revenue is increasing. The problem is not top-line. Direct the analysis toward the cost side.

questions.prompt: Compare the price per ounce of each SKU. Is the plastic gallon priced appropriately relative to the carton?
questions.guidance: A strong answer calculates price per ounce for both SKUs and notes that the gallon is actually cheaper per ounce despite higher production costs. Carton: $2.50 / 18 oz = ~$0.139/oz. Gallon: $4.00 / 36 oz = ~$0.111/oz. The gallon is priced 20% cheaper per ounce, yet costs more to produce.

math.setup: Compare unit price per ounce: carton at $2.50 for 18 oz vs gallon at $4.00 for 36 oz
steps: Difference: gallon is ~$0.028/oz cheaper despite higher production costs
math.answer: The gallon is priced ~20% cheaper per ounce than the carton, yet costs more to produce — a clear pricing problem.

questions.prompt: How are costs allocated across the two products? Is this appropriate?
questions.guidance: The producer uses a simple per-unit average: total factory costs divided by total units. This is the core problem — it allocates the same overhead and cost burden to both cartons and gallons regardless of the true cost to produce each. Plastic packaging is more expensive than paper cartons, and the gallon machine requires more skilled (higher-cost) labor. These incremental costs are being averaged into the carton cost rather than assigned to the gallons.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the sales mix on profitability?
questions.guidance: Gallons now represent 60% of sales. Because gallons are under-priced relative to their true cost, the more gallons sold, the more money is lost on each unit. The 20% volume growth amplifies the loss: growing volume in the highest-margin-destroying SKU accelerates profit erosion despite rising total revenue.

math.setup: Qualitative: if each gallon sold at a loss (revenue < true cost), then 60% of a growing volume base generates growing losses
steps: Each additional gallon sold at under-cost price widens the profit gap
Result: profits decline even as revenue grows
math.answer: The combination of under-pricing and rising gallon share means each year's volume growth destroys more profit than the prior year.

brainstorming.prompt: What other cost or operational issues should the firm investigate beyond the pricing and cost allocation problem already identified?

categories.name: Direct Costs
ideas: Raw material cost differences between paper carton and plastic jug
Incremental labor cost for operating the gallon machine vs. carton machine
Material waste or yield differences between the two packaging formats

categories.name: Overhead Allocation
ideas: Machine depreciation for the new gallon equipment
Maintenance costs specific to the gallon machine
Floor space or storage cost differences between the two SKUs

categories.name: Pricing Strategy
ideas: Activity-based costing to assign true overhead to each SKU
Volume-based discounts that may erode gallon margins further
Competitor pricing benchmarks for per-ounce juice pricing

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Production line efficiency and changeover costs
Inventory carrying costs if gallon turnover differs from carton
Retailer shelf space and logistics costs by SKU

recommendation: Conduct a thorough activity-based costing (ABC) analysis to identify the true direct and overhead costs attributable to each product (18 oz carton vs. 36 oz gallon)

Re-price the plastic gallon product to fully reflect its higher packaging material, labor, and equipment costs — the gallon price should exceed the carton on a per-ounce basis given its higher cost structure

Re-evaluate the overhead allocation methodology: replace the simple per-unit average with cost-driver-based allocation (e.g., machine hours, labor hours) to ensure each SKU carries its fair share of costs
risks: Re-pricing gallons upward may reduce demand for the gallon format, which has been driving volume growth
Customers may resist price increases if competitors offer cheaper gallon options
Transition to ABC may require significant management time and accounting system changes
next_steps: Perform full ABC analysis across both product lines immediately
Model profitability at various price points for the gallon SKU to find the profit-maximizing price
Monitor sales mix and margin by SKU on a monthly basis going forward
